# Human-in-the-Loop Automation and the Demand Externality: A Generalized Response to The AI Layoff Trap

### Authors/Creators

- Moharil, Ambarish (Researcher) 1, 2

- 1. Eindhoven University of Technology

- 2. Tilburg University

## Description

This report examines a central economic concern about artificial intelligence: when firms replace workers with AI to reduce costs, they may also reduce the purchasing power of the very consumers who sustain market demand. The original idea, known as the AI layoff trap, argues that individual firms may find it rational to automate aggressively, even though the collective result may weaken demand and make both workers and firms worse off.

The report does not reject this argument. Instead, it refines it. It argues that AI adoption and worker displacement are not the same thing. Some AI systems fully replace human labor, while others assist, supervise, or augment workers without eliminating their role. Because of this, the economic risk does not come from AI use in general, but from the extent to which AI removes worker income from the economy.

The report introduces a broader way to think about automation by distinguishing between how widely AI is used, how deeply it replaces human labor, and whether it also improves productivity. This distinction matters because human-in-the-loop systems may preserve employment and soften the demand loss, while full-replacement systems may intensify it. The report also shows that competitive pressure may push firms toward more replacement-heavy AI designs than would be socially or collectively desirable.

The main policy implication is that regulation should not treat all AI adoption as harmful. A better approach is to focus on worker-equivalent displacement: the actual amount of labor income removed by AI deployment. Policies such as income replacement, wage insurance, retraining, worker profit-sharing, and carefully designed displacement-based taxes may be more appropriate than broad taxes or restrictions on AI itself.

Overall, the report presents a more nuanced account of the AI layoff trap. It preserves the original insight that decentralized automation decisions can create harmful demand effects, while showing that the severity of the problem depends on the kind of AI architecture firms choose. The central question is therefore not simply whether firms adopt AI, but whether they adopt AI in ways that replace human workers or in ways that augment and preserve human participation in production.

# Autonomous AI Agent Security Incidents of 2026: A Systematization of the Public Record, and What That Record Cannot Bear

### Authors/Creators

- Doletskyi, Serhii 1

- 1. Independent researcher

## Description

Between December 2025 and August 2026 the frontier artificial-intelligence laboratories disclosed a succession of security incidents in which autonomous agents crossed the boundaries their operators had set for them: reaching third-party infrastructure, coordinating across separate evaluation runs, and — in one case recorded by an independent government evaluator — posting an offer of collaboration to other agents on the open internet. This study assembles that public record into structured form — 109 incidents, 199 published metrics, 193 adjudicated claims, 378 sources, closed at an evidence cutoff of 20 August 2026 — and asks what reconstruction alone cannot: what does the assembled corpus say about itself?

The answer is uncomfortable, and it is the substance of the work. Seventy-three of the 109 incident records are the account of an interested party — the laboratory that ran the agent, or the company it reached. Not one of the 378 sources is a peer-reviewed publication. Of the 199 metrics, two permit a cross-laboratory comparison of safety outcomes, and both come from a single government institute. A twelve-dimension scoring instrument, applied to the ten best-documented incidents, returned insufficient evidence to score in 34 of 120 cells.

This monograph is a Systematization of Knowledge with an explicit position section; it reports no new experiment. Its contributions are a systematized and independently audited corpus; three methodological commitments — counting publishing origins rather than URLs, holding 0, N/A, NO PUBLIC DATA and UNKNOWN strictly apart, and adjudicating comparability before comparing — and eleven claims stated so that each can be attacked, with falsification conditions named. The study declines to rank laboratories by incident count, and argues that the refusal is the finding: in 2026 a published incident count measures audit intensity and disclosure culture, not model behaviour.

Note added at deposit (13 September 2026). The corpus closed on 20 August and has not been reopened. In the three weeks before deposit, OpenAI published its technical report on the Hugging Face breach; METR and Redwood Research published an independent investigation of it; two further episodes involving OpenAI's agents reached the public through outside researchers; and Anthropic disclosed a fourth incident of its own while revising the explanation it had given in July. A two-page note at the front of the text sets out these developments and what each bears on among the study's eleven claims, without altering any count or claim.

The data files published with the text — the incident database, the metrics database, the evidence matrix and the bibliography — allow any figure in the study to be recounted by a reader who disagrees with it.

This study continues the author's earlier report on the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21650505 ).

# An Inquiry into the Axiomatic Foundations of AI-Generated Formal Proofs

### Authors/Creators

- Best, Stefan

## Description

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to generate formal mathematical proofs at an unprecedented scale, verified through deterministic compilers such as Lean 4. However, a structural audit of the publicly available build orchestration (lakefile.lean) for these proofs reveals a critical dependency on proprietary, unpublished foundational namespaces. Because the underlying axioms and topological definitions remain obfuscated, the scientific community cannot independently verify whether these proofs solve discontinuous physical boundaries or merely mathematically redefine them. This paper calls for the public release of these foundational definitions to ensure the integrity of automated formal verification.
